meta.title: Understanding the posterior
reference.title: Further reading
reference.text: Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern, David B. Dunson, Aki Vehtari and Donald B. Rubin, Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., CRC Press, 2013, chapters 1–2.
content.0: The posterior $\operatorname{Beta}(10,4)$ describes uncertainty about the coin’s success probability after the data are observed. A summary makes this distribution easier to interpret, but does not replace the distribution itself.
content.2: The posterior mean is $10/14\approx0.714$. The posterior mode, the maximum a posteriori estimate, is $(10-1)/(10+4-2)=0.75$. The posterior mean minimizes expected squared error loss; the appropriate summary depends on the decision and its loss function.
content.4: An equal-tailed 95% credible interval uses the 2.5% and 97.5% posterior quantiles. Conditional on the chosen model, prior and observed data, the posterior probability that $p$ lies within this interval is 0.95.
content.6: A frequentist 95% confidence interval uses a procedure that covers a fixed parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions. See the course’s confidence interval lesson for that interpretation.
content.8: The posterior predictive probability of success on the next trial is $E[p\mid x]=10/14\approx0.714$. This prediction averages over posterior uncertainty about $p$.
